¶
'''warning-wheel''' (wâr′ning-hwēl), ''n.'' In ''horol.'', a warning-piece in the form of a wheel.

'''warnish†, warnise†,''' ''v. t.'' Middle English forms of ''garnish''.
{{smaller block|<poem>He wiȝtly hem of-sent,
& het hem alle hiȝe thider as harde as thei miȝt,
Wel ''warnished'' for the werre with clene hors & armes.</poem>
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1083.}}}}

'''war-office''' (wâr′of″is), ''n.'' A public office or department in which military affairs are superintended or administered. {{smaller|(''a'') The department or bureau of the British government presided over by the Secretary of State for War, assisted by a parliamentary, a permanent, and a financial under secretary. It is subdivided into various departments, as the military, ordnance, and financial. (''b'') In the United States, the War Department.}}

'''warp''' (wârp), ''v.'' [(''a'') Trans., cast, throw, < ME. ''werpen'', ''weorpen'', ''worpen'' (pret. ''warp'', pp. ''worpen''), < AS. ''weorpan'' (pret. ''wearp''), cast, throw, = OS. ''werpan'' = D. MLG. ''werpen'' = OHG. ''werfan'', MHG. G. ''werfen'', throw, cast, = Icel. ''verpa'' = Goth. ''wairpan'', throw; cf. Lith. ''werpti'', spin, Gr. ῥέπειν, incline downward, ῥίπτειν, throw. (''b'') < ME. ''warpen'' (pret. ''warped''), < Icel. ''varpa'', throw, cast, also cast or lay out a net, = Sw. ''varpa'' = Dan. ''varpe'', warp (a ship), < ''varp'', a casting, also a cast with a net, also a warping, = Sw. ''varp'', the draft of a net, = Dan. ''varp'', a warp; from the strong verb above.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To cast; throw; hurl.
{{smaller block|Wente to hys wardrope, and ''warpe'' of hys wedez.
{{right|''Morte Arthure'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 901.}}
<poem>Ful sone it was ful loude kid
Of Havelok, how he ''warp'' the ston
Ouer the londes euerichon.    ''Havelok'', l. 1061.</poem>}}
readings.c2s3:
'''2†.''' To utter; ejaculate; enunciate; give utterance to.
{{smaller block|<poem>
Hit fyrst mynged,
Wylde wordez hym ''warp'' wyth a wrast noyce.
</poem>
{{right|''Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1423.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>
A note ful nwe I herde hem ''warpe'',
To lysten that watz ful lufly dere.
</poem>
{{right|''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), i. 878.}}}}

'''3.''' To bring forth (young) prematurely: said of cattle, sheep, horses, etc. [Prov. Eng.]—'''4.''' In ''rope-making'', to run (the yarn of the winches) into hauls to be tarred. See ''haul of yarn'', under ''haul''.—'''5.''' To weave; hence, in a figurative sense, to fabricate; plot.
{{smaller block|<poem>
But now; How, Where, of What shall I begin
This Gold-grownd Web to weave, to ''warp'', to spin?
</poem>
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Battle of Ivry.}}}}
{{smaller block|She acquainted the Greeks underhand with this treason, which was a ''warping'' against them.
{{right|''Holland'', tr. of Plutarch, p. 409.}}}}

'''6.''' To give a cast or twist to; turn or twist out of shape or out of straightness, as by unequal contraction, etc.; contort.
{{smaller block|<poem>
Oh, state of Nature, fail together in me,
Since thy best props are ''warp’d'' !
</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher (and another)'', Two Noble Kinsmen, iii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>
Confess, or I will ''warp''
Your limbs with such keen tortures ——.
</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', The Cenci, v. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|The cracked door, ill-fitting and ''warped'' from its original shape, guided us by a score of glittering crevices to the room we sought.
{{right|''D. Christie Murray'', Weaker Vessel, xxxiii.}}}}

{{smaller block|<poem>My favour here begins to ''warp.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., i. 2. 365.}}}}
'''4†.''' To weave; hence, to plot.
{{smaller block|<poem>Who like a fleering slavish parasite,
In ''warping'' profit or a traitorous sleight,
Hoops round his rotten body with devotes.</poem>
{{right|''Marlowe'', Hero and Leander, vi.}}}}
'''5.''' To fly with a twisting or bending to this side and that; deflect the course of flight; turn about in flying, as birds or insects.
{{smaller block|<poem>As when the potent rod
Of Amram’s son, in Egypt’s evil day,
Wav’d round the coast, up called a pitchy cloud
Of locusts ''warping'' on the eastern wind.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., i. 341.}}}}
'''6.''' To wind yarn off bobbins, to form the warp of a web. See the quotation.
{{smaller block|''Warping'', therefore, consists in arranging the threads according to number and colour, or in any special manner that may be necessary, and to keep them in their relative places after they have been so laid.
{{right|''A. Barlow'', Weaving, p. 68.}}}}
'''7.''' To slink; cast the young prematurely, as cows.—'''8.''' ''Naut.'', to work forward by means of a rope fastened to something fixed, as in moving from one berth to another in a harbor, or in making one’s way out of a harbor in a calm, or against a contrary wind.
{{smaller block|I gat out of the Mole of Chio into the sea by ''warping'' foorth, with the helpe of Genoueses botes.
{{right|''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', II. 101.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|warp|6826|warp}}</noinclude>nian, ''warnian'', take heed, warn, = OHG. ''warnōn'', warn, ''warnēn'' (''wernēn''), MHG. ''warnen'', provide, take heed, protect, warn, G. ''warnen'', warn, = Icel. ''varna'' = Sw. ''varna'', warn (cf. OF. ''warnir'', ''guarnir'', ''garnir'', provide, garnish, preserve, > ult. E. ''garnish'', ''garniture'', etc.); (''b'') < ME. ''wernen'', < AS. ''wyrnan'', refuse, deny, = OS. ''wernian'' = OHG. ''warnen'' = OFries. ''warna'', ''werna'' = Icel. ''varna'', refuse, deny; from the noun: see ''warn'', ''n.''] '''1.''' To put on guard by timely notice; wake, ware, or give notice to beforehand, as of approaching danger or of something to be avoided or guarded against; caution; admonish; tell or command admonishingly; advise.
{{smaller block|<poem>The doubt of future foes exiles my present ioy,
And wit me ''warnes'' to shun such snares as threaten mine annoy.</poem>
{{right|''Queen Elizabeth'', quoted in Puttenham’s Arte of Eng. [Poesie, Int., p. xii.}}}}
{{smaller block|Being ''warned'' by God in a dream that they should not return to Herod, they departed into their own country another way.
{{right|Mat. ii. 12.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And then I fear’d
Lest the gray navy there would splinter on it,
And fearing waved my arm to ''warn'' them off.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Sea Dreams.}}}}
'''2.''' To admonish, as to any duty; advise; expostulate with.
{{smaller block|''Warn'' them that are unruly.
{{right|1 Thes. v. 14.}}}}
'''3.''' To apprise; give notice to; make ware or aware; inform previously; notify; direct; bid; summon.
{{smaller block|William & hise wiȝes were ''warned'' of here come.
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 4288.}}}}
{{smaller block|Er the sun vp soght with his softe beames, <poem>Pelleus full prestly the peopull did ''warne''
To appere in his presens, princes and dukys.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1092.}}}}
{{smaller block|Who is it that hath ''warn’d'' us to the walls?
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, ii. 1. 201.}}}}
{{smaller block|The Bishop of Ross is ''warn’d'' by the Lords of the Council, that he shall no longer be esteem’d an Ambassador, but be punish’d as his Fault shall deserve.
{{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 345.}}}}
'''4†.''' To deny; refuse; forbid.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thou canst not ''warne'' him that with good entente
Axeth thyn help.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', A. B. C., l. 11.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The kynges hed, when hyt ys broȝt,
A kysse wyll y ''warne'' the noght,
For lefe to me hyt were!</poem>
{{right|''Octavian'' (ed. Halliwell), l. 821.}}}}
'''5†.''' To defend; keep or ward off. ''Spenser.''

'''warner''' (wâr′nėr), ''n.'' '''1.''' One who or that which warns; an admonisher.—'''2.''' See the quotation.
{{smaller block|Sotiltees . . . were nothing more than devices in sugar and paste, which, in general, . . . had some allusion to the circumstances of the entertainment, and closed the service of the dishes. The ''warners'' were ornaments of the same nature, which preceded them.
{{right|''R. Warner'', Antiquitates Culinariæ (ed. 1791), p. 136, note.}}}}

'''warnesture†''', ''v. t.''   [ME., < OF. ''warnesture'', ''garnesture'', ''garnisture'', ''garniture'', provision, stores, furniture, garniture: see ''garniture''.]   To furnish; store.
{{smaller block|<poem>Wel thei were ''warnestured'' of vitayles i-now,
plentiuosly for al peple to passe where thei wold.</poem>
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1121.}}}}
{{smaller block|I shal ''warnestoore'' myn hous with toures, swiche as han castelles and other manere edifices, and armure and artelries.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Tale of Melibeus.}}}}

'''warning''' (wâr′ning), ''n.''   [< ME. ''warninge'', a warning, admonition, < AS. ''wearnung'' (= OHG. ''warnunge'', G. ''warnung'', a warning), verbal n. of ''wearnian'', ''warnian'', warn: see ''warn'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' Notice beforehand of the consequences that will probably follow continuance in some particular course; admonitory advice to do or to abstain from doing something, as in reference to approaching a probable danger.
{{smaller block|Hear the word at my mouth, and give them ''warning'' from me.
{{right|Ezek. iii. 17.}}}}
'''2.''' That which warns, or serves to warn or admonish.
{{smaller block|Let Christian’s slips before he came hither, and the battles that he met with in this place, be a ''warning'' to those that come after.
{{right|''Bunyan'', Pilgrim’s Progress, ii.}}}}
'''3.''' Heed; the lesson taught by or to be learned from a caution given.
{{smaller block|I think it is well that they stand so near the highway, that others may see and take ''warning''.
{{right|''Bunyan'', Pilgrim’s Progress, ii.}}}}
'''4.''' Previous notice: as, a short ''warning''.
{{smaller block|Somewhat too sudden, sirs, the ''warning'' is.
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., v. 2. 14.}}}}
'''5.''' A summons; a call; a bidding.
{{smaller block|It [sherris] illumineth the face, which as a beacon gives ''warning'' . . . to arm.
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., iv. 3. 117.}}}}
'''6.''' A notice given to terminate a business relation, as that of master and servant, employer and employee, landlord and tenant; a notice to quit.

{{smaller block|Servants in husbandry [23 Hen. VI., c. 12] are required to give their masters ''warning'', and to engage with some other master before quitting their present service.
{{right|''Ribton-Turner'', Vagrants and Vagrancy, p. 66.}}}}

'''warning''' (wâr′ning), ''p. a.'' In ''biol.'', serving as a menace to enemies; of threatening aspect: somewhat specially used of a strikingly conspicuous coloration. See the quotation.
{{smaller block|A never-failing interest attaches to the subject of ''Warning Colors.'' The history of the discovery of ''warning'' colors in caterpillars is quoted with many examples, showing that the education of enemies is assisted by the fact that ''warning'' colors and patterns often resemble each other, and there is abundant evidence to show that insect-eating animals learn by experience.
{{right|''Amer. Nat.'', Oct., 1890, p. 929.}}}}

'''warningly''' (wâr′ning-li), ''adv.'' In a warning manner; so as to warn; by way of notice or admonition.

'''warning-piece''' (wâr′ning-pēs), ''n.'' Something that warns. {{smaller|(''a'') A warning-gun; a signal-gun; the discharge of a cannon intended as a notification. Compare ''piece'', 4 (''b'').}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Hark! upon my life, the knight! ’tis your friend;
This was the ''warning-piece'' of his approach.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Wit at Several Weapons, v. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|The treason of Watson and Cleark, two English seminaries, is sufficiently known; it was as a “prælludium” or ''warning-piece'' to the great “fougade,” the discharge of the powder-treason.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), II. 97.}}}}
{{smaller block|(''b'') In ''horol.'', a part of the striking-mechanism of a clock that, by the movement of the lower wheel, throws the striking-system periodically into action. It is also operated by the strike-or-silent mechanism, so that the striking-mechanism may be thrown out of gear at will. When in position to work, it causes a slight noise at the instant of starting the striking-parts, and thus gives warning that the clock is about to strike.}}

'''warning-wheel''' (wâr′ning-hwēl), ''n.'' In ''horol.'', a warning-piece in the form of a wheel.

{{smaller block|The cracked door, ill-fitting and ''warped'' from its original shape, guided us by a score of glittering crevices to the room we sought.

'''7.''' To turn aside from the true direction; cause to bend or incline; pervert.
{{smaller block|This first avowed, nor folly ''warped'' my mind.
{{right|''Dryden'', Sig. and Guis., l. 402.}}}}
{{smaller block|By the present mode of education we are forcibly ''warped'' from the bias of nature.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Taste.}}}}
{{smaller block|His heart was form’d for softness — ''warp’d'' to wrong.
{{right|''Byron'', Corsair, iii. 23.}}}}
{{smaller block|Men’s perceptions are ''warped'' by their passions.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', Social Statics, p. 182.}}}}

'''8.''' ''Naut.'', to move into some desired place or position by hauling on a rope or warp which has been fastened to something fixed, as a buoy, anchor, or other ship at or near that place or position: as, to ''warp'' a ship into harbor or to her berth.
{{smaller block|They ''warped'' out their ships by force of hand.
{{right|''Mir. for Mags.'', p. 881.}}}}
{{smaller block|Seeing them ''warp'' themselues to windward, we thought it not good to be boorded on both sides at an anchor.
{{right|Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith’s'' Works, II. 41.}}}}

'''9.''' In ''agri.'', to fertilize, as poor or barren land, by means of artificial inundation from rivers which hold large quantities of earthy matter, or warp (see ''warp'', ''n.'', 4), in suspension. {{smaller|The operation, which consists in inclosing a body or sheet of water till the sediment it holds in suspension has been deposited, can be carried out only on flat low-lying tracts which may be readily submerged. This system was first systematically practised in Great Britain on the banks of the Trent, Ouse, and other rivers which empty into the estuary of the Humber.}}

'''10.''' To change. [Rare.]
<poem>Freeze, freeze, thou bitter sky,
Thou dost not bite so nigh
As benefits forgot;
Though thou the waters ''warp'',
Thy sting is not so sharp
As friend remember’d not.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, ii. 7. 187.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To turn, twist, or be twisted out of straightness or the proper shape.
{{smaller block|After the manner of wood that curbeth and ''warpeth'' with the fire. {{right|''Holland'', tr. of Plutarch, p. 561.}}}}
{{smaller block|It ’s better to shoot in a bow that has been shot in before, and will never start, than to draw a fair new one, that for every arrow will be ''warping''.
{{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, v. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Ye are green wood, see ye ''warp'' not.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, ii.}}}}
'''2.''' To turn or incline from a straight, true, or proper course; deviate; swerve.
{{smaller block|<poem>There is our commission,
From which we would not have you ''warp''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., i. 1. 15.}}}}
{{smaller block|Now, by something I had lately observed of Mr. Treasurer’s conversation on occasion, I suspected him a little ''warping'' to Rome. {{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, May 17, 1671.}}}}
{{smaller block|By and by, as soon as the shadow of Sir Francis hath left him, he fals off again ''warping'' and ''warping'' till he come to contradict himselfe in diameter; and denies flatly that it is either variable or arbitrary, being once settl’d.
{{right|''Milton'', Apology for Smectymnuus.}}}}
{{smaller block|Whatever these ''warping'' Christians might pretend as to zeal for the Law and their ancient Religion, the bottom of all was a principle of infidelity.
{{right|''Stillingfleet'', Sermons, II. iii.}}}}
'''3.''' To change for the worse; turn in a wrong direction.
{{smaller block|<poem>Methinks My favour here begins to ''warp.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., i. 2. 365.}}}}
